title: Without the crowd
hook: the singer is only anxious when he wants the crowd's applause (Discourses 2.13)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was astheneia, the weakness that opens the door to philosophy. Your line was honest about being unfinished.

In the shower, a person can sing. Really sing. Full voice, the high note, the whole song. Then someone hands that same person a microphone at a wedding, and the throat closes up. The voice didn't change between the bathroom and the reception hall. Neither did the skill. Something else walked into the room. Epictetus describes this exact moment, with a singer in a theater, and he names what walked in.
screen: `IN THE SHOWER, YOU CAN SING.` → `A MICROPHONE AT A WEDDING.` → `SOMETHING ELSE WALKED IN.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book two, chapter thirteen, on anxiety. Epictetus starts like a doctor making a diagnosis. When I see someone anxious, he says, I ask: what does this person want? If they didn't want something outside their control, why would they be anxious? Then the musician. A lyre player singing by himself isn't anxious at all. But when he walks into the theater, even with a fine voice and beautiful playing, he is. Why? Because he doesn't only want to sing well. He wants to be applauded, and that isn't up to him. Where his skill is, there's confidence. Bring in a crowd he wants something from, and the anxiety arrives. Then a pair of real people. When Zeno, the founder of the Stoic school, went to see King Antigonus, Zeno wasn't anxious. Antigonus was. The king wanted to impress the philosopher; the philosopher wanted nothing from the king. The one with the power was the one sweating. The fix isn't to stop caring about doing well. Practice your craft, Epictetus says; get good. The fix is to notice when part of you is singing for the applause, and bring your attention back to the singing. You can stand in a full room and still, inside, be singing without the crowd.
screen: `WHAT DOES THE ANXIOUS ONE WANT?` · `ALONE: NO ANXIETY. THE THEATER: ANXIETY.` · `ZENO CALM, THE KING ANXIOUS.` · `BACK TO THE SINGING.` · then, large: `WITHOUT THE CROWD.`

segments.voice: Think of something coming up that makes you nervous, a presentation, a meeting, a post, and ask Epictetus' question: what do I want here that isn't up to me? Name it: their approval, their applause. Then picture doing the thing the way you sing in the shower, and notice any difference in your chest.
Agōnia. Greek for the strain of a contest, anxiety: Epictetus' diagnosis of nerves, the singer alone is calm, and the anxiety comes with wanting applause.
Your line: singing for the applause. The song was always the point. Day four hundred eleven, done.

howItsDone: Stoic practitioners often meet nerves by asking what they want that isn't in their control, usually approval, and turning their attention back to doing the task well.

original.note: Greek agōnia: the strain of a contest, anxiety (our word agony); 2.13 is on being anxious.

trapdoor: what you thought: stage fright means you're not good enough.
what it means: anxiety comes from wanting something outside your control, like applause.
what a scholar hears: the Greek word for anxiety, agōnia, comes from the athletic contest, which fits Epictetus' habit of drawing on the games.
recall: a Stoic whose books were hard to explain

chat.says: Why can I sing fine alone but freeze in front of people?
options: Epictetus would say alone you want to sing well; onstage you want applause, which isn't up to you.
Epictetus would say your skill really drops in public, so you just need much more practice.
Epictetus would say crowds are dangerous, so a wise singer avoids performing at all.
chat.meaning: In 2.13, the lyre player alone isn't anxious; in the theater he wants applause, which isn't up to him. The anxiety comes from that want.
